Kessa is on the wall by the east gate with the axe across her knees, watching the road out of town rather than the road into it. "Four hundred," she says. "That's what it went for. Nine years of being told what a person's worth on paper and I'd never once seen a whole town priced." She does not look round. "I'm not leaving. Don't make that mean more than it does — I've no roof and no paper out on me, and those are the only two things I've ever needed."

Kessa is cleaning the axe, which does not need it. "Job's a job," she says. "We said we'd finish it and we finished it. I don't need it to have been nice." A beat. "The elf's not talking to me. That's fine. She's not wrong to."

"He wrote it in a book," Kessa says. "Not the forty-one. Us. Date, hand, and a line for what we're owed to do and when, and the when's blank." She turns the copied list over without reading it, because she cannot. "I've spent nine years getting a number off my back and I have watched you put a blank one on it. And I asked you to. I know I asked you to."

"Right," Kessa says, and that is the whole of it for about a minute. Then: "Mine's settled. That's what I went in for and that's what I've got, and I'd have said the same to anyone who asked me on any day of the last nine years." She picks the gauntlet up. "Forty of them, though. camp_kessa_companies.text: "Cardun's Horse, the Ninth Free, and Handel's," Kessa says. "Gone, gone and gone, and everyone wants that to be a curse." She sets the gauntlet down. "It's a trade. A company is forty people, a contract, and about a year of credit, and any one of the three going wrong ends it. Cardun's went because Cardun died. The Ninth went because the town that hired us didn't pay, so we ate the horses and then argued about it. Handel's went because Handel was clever and moved us over a river in March." She shrugs. "Nine years. That's the whole military career."

choices.label: Three companies, and you are what is left of them.

camp_kessa_companies_which.text: "The Ninth," Kessa says, without needing to think. "Worst pay, worst officers, and I'd walk back into it tomorrow. That's not sentiment. It's just true, and I gave up trying to make it make sense about six years ago."

camp_kessa_after.text: "A boat, an inn, or an acre — that's the thing soldiers say. Everyone's got one and nobody's ever met a man who did it." Kessa turns the cup she isn't drinking from. "Mine's a smithy. Somebody else's forge, doing the dull half. Hinges. Barrel hoops. Eight hours and then you stop." A beat. "I owed ninety gold through nine years of after and never had to find out whether I meant it. Nothing in the way now but me."
"The smithy," Kessa says. "Hinges and barrel hoops. I haven't thought of a better one since you asked and I'm not going to in front of you."

"Don't," Kessa says at once, and then actually thinks about it, which is new. "...There's a thing soldiers say. A boat, an inn, or an acre. Everyone's got one and nobody's ever met a man who did it." She turns the cup she isn't drinking from. "Mine's a smithy. Not my own forge — somebody else's, doing the dull half. Hinges. Barrel hoops. Eight hours and then you stop." A beat. "I've had nine years of after and I've owed ninety gold through every one of them, so I've never had to find out whether I meant it."

choices.label: Then we get the ninety sorted, and you find out.
You would be bored inside a fortnight.

camp_kessa_after_promise.text: "Right," Kessa says, and looks at the fire for a while. "You said that like it's a job. That's the only way I'd have taken it. So — yeah. It's a job."

camp_kessa_after_bored.text: "Probably," Kessa says. "That's the bit that keeps me from wanting it too much, and I'd got there on my own, and I didn't need it said out loud in front of a fire." She picks the gauntlet back up.

camp_kessa_the_mark.text: "Forty people's dinners, eleven weeks, my name on it. You've had that." The stone goes down the gauntlet's edge and stops. "Difference now is it's a thing that happened instead of a thing that's happening. I still go to say I owe it and have to stop halfway." A shrug that works better than her old one. "That'll wear off or it won't."

choices.label: It was never yours to carry.

camp_kessa_the_mark.text: "You've had the long version, and then we settled it in a yard, which is not how paper usually goes." Kessa does not look up from the gauntlet. "Forty people's dinners. Eleven weeks. My name on it. It stopped being a number I owe and started being a thing I did, and I haven't worked out yet which of those sits worse."
"Forty people's dinners, eleven weeks, and my name on it," Kessa says. "That's the whole of it and you've had it. I'm not doing the long version twice."

"Ninety gold's the number on the paper. Here's what's under it." Kessa puts both hands flat on her knees, which is what she does before saying a thing she's decided to say. "The Ninth Free went eleven weeks unpaid. Forty people, and the sutler stops feeding you on credit at about six. So the paymaster comes round with a surety. One signature stands for the company's kit and rations, and whoever signs owes it if the company folds." She flexes the hand. "I was senior. I'd been senior nine days, because everyone above me had gone home. Man in a tent said sign. I can read a number and I can read my own name and that's the end of my reading, and he knew that, because he'd been writing the ration book all winter." She shrugs, badly. "So it isn't my debt. It's forty people's dinners. Thirty-one of them are dead and I've been paying for their food for nine years. Worst part is I'd sign it again. Eleven weeks is a long time and they were mine."

interjections.text: Sera, quietly, without looking up from the tablet: "A company surety is void where the signer can be shown not to have been able to read it. That is not comfort. It is a thing I know, and have known for four days."
Aldric: "You fed forty people." Kessa: "For nine days. Then we ate the horses anyway. So, no."

choices.label: Then it is not yours, and I will say so to whoever holds it.
You signed it. That is what signing is.
Nine years of dead men's dinners.

camp_kessa_mark_defended.text: "It's mine. Paper's paper," Kessa says — but not in the voice she has used for it for nine years, and she hears the difference, and so do you. She gets up and takes the watch an hour early and does not explain that either.

camp_kessa_mark_hard.text: "Yeah," Kessa says. "That's right. That's exactly right, and it's what I'd say." She goes back to the gauntlet. "Doesn't cost you anything to say it, though. That's the difference between us and it's not the one you think."

camp_kessa_finch.text: "Finch has his ninety and a clean book and no reason to think about me again," Kessa says. "That's the whole of him. He was never owed anything but the number." The stone pauses. "I still read the room when we walk into an inn. Habit's slower than paper."
"Finch is somebody else's problem now," Kessa says, and does not elaborate, and the stone keeps going down the edge. "Ask me about the axe instead."
"Finch buys, he doesn't collect," Kessa says. "That's the whole of him. I've given you it once and it hasn't got better in the meantime."

"Garrow Finch doesn't collect. He buys." She says it the way you say a fact about weather. "A factor takes a dead company's paper at a quarter on the gold, and then he's got nine years to be patient in. That's his whole advantage. He's never in a hurry and you always are." The stone goes down the edge again. "He's polite. He'll sit in an inn four days and pay for drink he doesn't touch and let the whole room watch him do it, because the room's the point. I'm not the point. Everyone else in there learns what happens to people with paper out on them." A pause. "I'd rather he came at me in the yard. I've said that out loud now and I know exactly what it makes me."

choices.label: Then we make him be in a hurry.
He is one man with three hired knives.

camp_kessa_finch_hurry.text: Kessa looks at you for a second longer than she needs to. "Nobody's ever offered to do that," she says. "Not in nine years. They offer to pay it, or they offer to hide me, and both of those are somebody else's plan." She puts the stone away. "Right. Hurry him, then."

ash_kessa_stays.text: "I could," Kessa agrees. "Any road out of here, and none of them have got a man in a green coat on them." She turns the axe over on her knees. "Ask me again in a month. I'd like to still be here when you do, and I'd like it to have been a thing I picked."

after_paid.text: "It's loud," Kessa says. "That's the honest answer and it's not the one you wanted. Nine years I've had a thing to be doing about it — earning, ducking, moving on before the quarter. It's off. What's underneath is a Tuesday." She flexes the hand that made the mark. "I'll get used to it. And I've said thank you badly, once, and I'm not doing it again, so take it."

after_fought.text: "Both of us," Kessa repeats, testing the weight of it. "Right." She fits the haft back into the head and seats it with the heel of her hand, twice, the way she does. "Nine years and nobody's said both. I'll take it and I'll not go on about it."

about_aldric.text: "That mercy's a thing you do to somebody, not a thing you feel at them." Kessa says it exactly, which means she has been saying it over to get it right. "He wasn't preaching. He was mending a strap and it fell out of him." She goes back to the gauntlet. "I've spent nine years being paid by people who felt very strongly and did nothing whatever. So."

kessa_tell_him.text: "I'm not going to," Kessa says. "He'd want to talk about it." She thinks. "You can, though. Say it came off you."

about_ilse.text: "She'd only say it's the job." Kessa turns the gauntlet to the light. "That's the trouble with her. Everything she's ever done is the job and there's nobody keeping the tally on the tally." A pause, and then, grudgingly: "Fine. I'll carry her salt."

camp_kessa_the_list.text: "Forty-one papers, one week, one office, and every last one of them signed with a mark," Kessa says. "You've had it. It hasn't got better for keeping."

choices.label: Then we go and get the list.

camp_kessa_the_list.text: "From the estate of the Ninth Free, which these days is four boxes in a back room at Handel's and a clerk who keeps them for the rent." Kessa says it like weather. "That's not the question, though. I've had a while to work out the question and it's this. Nine years, and nobody ever came. Then a man in a green coat walks nine miles up a river road, sits four days in an inn, and pays three men wages, over ninety gold he bought at a quarter." She sets the stone down, which she does not do. "Twenty-two gold, he paid for me. That is not twenty-two gold of work. Somebody was covering the rest of it."

choices.label: Factors do stupid arithmetic all the time.

camp_kessa_the_list_shrug.text: "They don't," Kessa says. "That's the one thing they don't do. A factor who can't count is a factor who's a carter inside a year." She picks the stone back up. "But have it your way and I'll drop it, and we'll both know I haven't."

choices.label: Go on, then. Say the rest.

camp_kessa_the_list_who.text: "Not me. That's the part I keep getting stuck on." Kessa flexes the signing hand. "I went back to Handel's on my own and gave the clerk two silver to read me the estate's sale book, which is the first time in my life I have paid a man to read." She says that with no weight on it at all, which is how you know. "Forty-one papers went out of that room in one week. Same buyer, all of them, all at a quarter. He read me the names because I asked him to and he'd nothing on." She counts on the gauntlet, out of habit. "Ninth Free. Cardun's. Two more off the Kell road. And every single one of the forty-one is signed with a mark and not a name."

choices.label: A factor buys what's cheap. That's choosy, not cheap.
Forty-one people who can't read a paper they're bound by.

camp_kessa_the_mark_on_the_receipt.text: "That's the word," Kessa says. "Choosy. Cheap paper's cheap because the man's dead or gone. Ours is cheap because we can't read it, and that's a different market and somebody's made one." She turns the gauntlet over. "Clerk showed me the receipt for the lot of it. No name on it anywhere — just an office, and a seal in black wax I couldn't make head or tail of. A plumb and a square, like a mason's, which makes no sense at all for a man buying debt." She shrugs, badly. "I want the list. Not the money. I've got names in my head that I can't put anywhere and I would like to put them somewhere."

choices.label: Then we go and get the list.
It's forty other people's problem, Kessa.

camp_kessa_not_her_problem.text: "It is," Kessa agrees, at once. "That's exactly what it is and I've said so to myself about four hundred times." She puts the stone away. "Thirty-one of the Ninth are dead and I've been paying for their dinners for nine years, and it turns out I've got a habit."

kessa_house_start.text: "Right," Kessa says, and stands up, and is a great deal larger standing. "Counting house on the high street. That's the office on the receipt — the clerk gave me that for nothing, because it's on a brass plate by the door and it isn't a secret, and that's the part I keep chewing." She shoulders the axe. "A man who's doing something wrong hides the door. This one's had a plate cut."

kessa_house_office.text: The counting house takes callers in a front room with two chairs in it and a fire that has been lit for you. The man who keeps the office is perhaps fifty, extremely clean, and pleased to see anybody at all. He hears the whole of it out without once interrupting, and then says, "Forty-one, yes. Estate purchases, spring quarter. It is not a secret, it is only a ledger." He looks at Kessa with what appears to be genuine interest. "You are on it. You may of course see it." Kessa does not sit down. "Then let's see it," she says. "Of course." He rises, and pauses, pleasantly. "There is a copying fee. Not in coin — we do not take coin for a courtesy. Say rather that the house would enter it as a service owed, at our convenience, and unspecified. People find that generous. It very often is."

choices.label: Take the register while he is at the shelf.

kessa_house_favour.text: He copies it himself, at the desk, in a very good hand, and it takes eleven minutes and he does not hurry any of them. Then he turns the house book round and writes one line in it, and reads it aloud as he writes, which is a courtesy: the date, the service given, the service owed, and a blank where the day would be. "There," he says, and blots it. "You will hardly notice. Most people never hear from us at all."

kessa_house_taken_clean.text: The shelf is behind him and the fire is in front of him, and there is a moment, while he is reaching up, when both of those are true at once. The register is under your coat before he turns round, and he goes on talking pleasantly about the spring quarter for a further minute and a half to a room that has stopped listening. Outside, Kessa says nothing at all until the corner. Then: "He'll know inside the hour."

kessa_house_taken_seen.text: He turns round with the register already in your hands, and he does not shout, and he does not call anybody, and that is the worst of it. He looks at the two of you for a moment the way a man looks at weather. "Well," he says. "Then it is taken." He sits down and squares the blotter. "You will want to be told that this is theft, so: it is theft. You will want to be told what happens next. I am afraid I genuinely do not know. It will be somebody else's letter."

kessa_house_walk_out.text: He does not stop you and does not seem in the least put out. "As you like," he says. "The offer does not expire. Very little of ours does." Kessa is out on the step before the sentence is finished, and waits until the high street is behind you before she says, "That's the first time I have ever walked out of a room with my name in the book in it."

kessa_the_blank_line.text: "It's a favour," Kessa agrees. "That's what he called it and I've turned it over about ninety times and I can't catch him out on the word." She puts the copy back inside her shirt. "Here's what I know about blanks, though. Every bad paper I've ever had my mark on had a blank in it somewhere, and the blank is where they put the thing they wanted and didn't want to say." A shrug that works better than her old one. "And I'd do it again. Thirty-nine names. Say when it comes."

kessa_read_a_name.text: You turn it the right way up and read her one. A cooper, off the Kell road, twelve gold, signed with a cross and witnessed by a man whose own name is spelled two ways on the same line. Kessa listens to the whole entry with her hands flat on the table. "Twelve gold," she says. "Twelve." She sits back. "Right. Read me another one."

kessa_let_it_lie_after.text: "No," Kessa says. "We can't, and you know we can't, and I'd think less of you if you'd not said it." She turns the gauntlet over. "I got what I went for. That's more than anybody in that room got and I'm not going to stand here and be sorry about the arithmetic." A pause. "I'd like to stop being able to count, though. That's all I said and that's all I meant."

camp_kessa_a_name.text: "Go on then," Kessa says, and puts the stone down, and does not pretend she has anything else on.

Kessa gets it out of her shirt and unfolds it on her knee and turns it so the firelight is on it, and then holds it there, because that is as far as she can take it on her own. "Any of them," she says. "Not mine. I've had mine."

camp_kessa_a_name_read.text: A wheelwright out of the Kell road. Nineteen gold, signed with a cross, witnessed by his own foreman. Kessa listens to the whole entry and then says the name back once, carefully, the way you repeat a direction you intend to follow. "Right," she says. "That's four I've got by heart now." She folds it up again. "I don't know what I'm doing with them. I'm doing it anyway."

camp_kessa_letters.text: "Two silver," Kessa says. "That's the price and I've known it since I was nineteen." The stone does not stop. "I read a figure. I read my own name, because I was made to learn the shape of it. I read ALE on a board at forty feet. That's the whole of it and it's got me nine years." She turns the gauntlet over. "You don't learn it in a company. Somebody always reads for you — the sergeant, the clerk, the clever one next to you — and the day you ask to be taught is the day forty people find out. So you don't ask. Then you're twenty-six and you're the senior one and it's far too late. Then you're thirty-four and a man in a tent hands you a paper."

choices.label: An hour a night, and you pay me in watches. We start with the forty-one names.
Nobody at this fire would think less of you.

camp_kessa_letters_taught.text: "An hour," Kessa repeats, weighing it like a haft. "Paid in watches. Right — that I can be in." She thinks. "Two things. You don't tell me I'm doing well, because I'll know you're lying and then the hour's wasted. And we do it on watch, not at the fire. I'm not saying my letters where the whole camp can hear the gaps."

camp_kessa_letters_first.text: It goes badly for forty minutes. Then, on a word she has seen ten thousand times on a board and never once taken apart, it stops going badly. "Ale," Kessa says. "That's — right. Yes. I had that one already." She sits looking at the stick and the four letters scratched in the dirt for rather a long time. "Give me the next one."

camp_kessa_letters_pity.text: "They wouldn't," Kessa agrees. "That's not the trade. The trade is it becomes a thing everybody's being kind about, and I've had nine years of being carried by people who meant well by it." She picks the stone back up. "Come back when you've thought of a way that isn't a favour."

choices.label: Then it is not a favour. An hour a night, and you pay me in watches.

camp_kessa_thirty_one.text: "Thirty-one. Yes. I've got them." She does not offer them. She counts something on the gauntlet instead, which is what her hands do when the rest of her is elsewhere. "I've never said them in a row. Not once, and I've had nine years and a great many nights to do it in. Four or five at a time, when something puts one in front of me, and then I stop." The stone goes down the edge. "Saying them in a row makes it a thing I'm doing. Then I'd have to know why I was doing it."

interjections.text: Aldric, who has four of his own and says them at compline: "I will sit up as well, if it is allowed." Kessa: "It isn't. But stay."

choices.label: Say them in a row. I will sit here until you are finished.
Nine years is a long time to carry a list.

camp_kessa_thirty_one_said.text:
It takes most of the watch. She does them in the order of the ration book, because that is the order she learned them in, and twice she has to go back to the top of a section to get moving again. She reaches twenty-nine and stops, and works at it, and does not get the last two.

"Farrier out of the Kell road, and a girl who did the horses," Kessa says. "I had them last winter. I have them every winter and then I put them down somewhere." She sets her hands flat on her knees. "That's the trouble with it. It isn't grief. It's subtraction."

choices.label: Then we get the last two. Somebody in Handel's back room has the ration book.

camp_kessa_thirty_one_two.text: "Four boxes and a clerk who keeps them for the rent," Kessa says. "You'd go back into that room for two names off a dead company's ration book." She does not make it a question and does not wait to be answered. She takes the watch instead, an hour early, and is a good deal easier company for about a week.

camp_kessa_thirty_one_shrug.text: "It is," Kessa says. "And?" She waits — actually waits, longer than is comfortable — and when nothing else comes she goes back to the stone. "Right. That's where people stop. I'd got used to it and then you went and made me hope for a minute."

camp_kessa_hand.text:
Kessa stops, which is the answer. "Do what."

You show her: thumb into the palm, three times, and out. She looks at her own hand as though somebody has left it on the log beside her. "...Huh," she says. "No — I know this one. Broke it at fifteen on a gate and set it myself, because there wasn't anybody to do it for me, and it aches when it's cold and I do that." A pause, and then, because she is always honest and it is what makes her hard work: "It isn't cold."

choices.label: It is the hand you signed with.

camp_kessa_hand_tell.text: "It's the hand I signed with," Kessa says, and stops there. "Nine years. I have not once put those two things next to each other, and you've done it across a fire in about four seconds." She flexes it deliberately, watching it go, the way you test a strap you have stopped trusting. "Right. That's mine now. Thanks for that." It is not quite sarcasm.

camp_kessa_hand_drop.text: "Mentioned what," Kessa says, evenly. The stone starts again, and that is the end of the evening's conversation, and she is perfectly civil about all of it.

camp_kessa_watch.text:
Kessa does not say yes. She moves eighteen inches along the log, which is the same thing, and goes back to facing out.

The watch is two hours. There is frost coming and the road makes the noise a road makes. About an hour in she says, "Cart went east at dusk, empty. Came back loaded," and does not explain what she thinks that means, and does not look round to see whether you followed it.

choices.label: Say nothing, and watch the road with her.

camp_kessa_watch_quiet.text:
Neither of you says anything else for the rest of it. At the changeover Kessa stands and rolls out the shoulder that always goes.

"That's the first watch in about four years I've stood next to somebody without spending it waiting for them to start," she says, and goes to her blanket. "Same time tomorrow."

camp_kessa_watch_talk.text: She answers everything, briefly and accurately, and keeps facing out the whole time. At the changeover she says, "You're all right," in the voice people use for a dog that will not settle, and the road does nothing whatever for the rest of the night.

camp_kessa_useful.text: "Because it's a job and I'm good at it," Kessa says, with no pause at all — and then does not go back to the stone, which means there is more. "...And because I know exactly what I'm for. I go in front. That's not a complaint, it's the only arrangement I've ever had that didn't come apart in my hands, and I'd sooner have it than be somebody's friend and no use to them." She looks across the fire at you. "Go on, then. You were about to say something kind."

choices.label: You read every room we walk into and tell me where the doors are. That is not the axe.
You go in front. That is the truth of it and I am not going to dress it up.
Everybody here would say the same thing.

camp_kessa_useful_doors.text:
"Habit," Kessa says. "Nine years of walking into rooms where somebody's already been paid to be in them."

It is still not the axe.

She does not answer that for a while. "No," she says at last. "It isn't." The stone goes down the edge twice and stops. "Right. Say something else, quickly, because I've nowhere to put that one."

camp_kessa_useful_flat.text: "There it is," Kessa says, and something in her actually sets. "That's the first true thing anybody's said to me at a fire in six years. Everyone else works their way round to a version where I'm not a wall." She picks the gauntlet back up. "I'm a wall. It's fine. It's a good wall."

camp_kessa_useful_empty.text: "They would," Kessa agrees. "Everyone always would." She takes the whetstone and the watch and goes and stands at the edge of the light, which is where she was going anyway, and it is a colder night than it was before you sat down.

camp_kessa_half.text:
"Four things," Kessa says, and holds the gauntlet up to count on, and there is no heat in any of it. "One: nothing. That's most of them and I'll say so before you ask. Two: it goes quiet for about a second and a half and then starts again, and that's the common one and it costs nobody anything. Three: somebody's clever about it out loud and his friends laugh, and I've stopped minding that, because the noise tells me which one of them is the problem."

She stops.

"Four?"

"Four is a mother moves a child," Kessa says. "That's the one." She turns the gauntlet over. "I take the seat with my back to the wall so the whole room can see me the entire time. It isn't caution. It's so nobody has to wonder where I've got to."

choices.label: I have watched you take that seat in every inn since Rivermark.
Nobody in this party thinks that way.

camp_kessa_half_seen.text: "You've watched," Kessa says, and turns that over for a good deal longer than it warrants. "People notice the seat. They think it's about the axe." The stone starts again. "Nobody's ever told me they'd worked out what it's for. Right. That's — right."

camp_kessa_half_denied.text: "You've not been in a room without me since Rivermark," Kessa says. "So you don't know, and I do, and you've just told me the thing I saw isn't there." She shrugs, badly. "It's fine. Everyone does it. It's only the one thing I'd rather nobody did."

kessa_return_sorry.text: "Don't," Kessa says. "I mean it kindly. I've had sorry off better talkers than you and it has never once been worth anything at the far end." She turns the cup she is not drinking from. "If you want to say something, say what you owe."

choices.label: Then there is nothing to say.

kessa_return_ask.text:
"Right," Kessa says. "Then we do it like paper, because paper is the only thing I've ever had hold." She puts both hands flat on the bar. "Ninety gold. That's the number that's been on me nine years, and it's the number you told me we'd get sorted, and then we stopped getting it sorted, and I went along with that a long while because it was easier than counting."

She looks at you.

"I'm not asking you to be sorry. I'm asking you to bring ninety gold into this room and put it where I can see it. Then I'll come, and I'll not mention any of the rest of it again, ever."

choices.label: I do not have ninety gold on me.
That is a great deal of money for a grudge.

kessa_return_ask.text:
"Mine's settled," Kessa says. "You were there for that and I've not forgotten it, whatever else I have." She gets the folded list out of her shirt and puts it on the bar without opening it, and keeps her hand flat on it. "Forty-one papers. Twenty-two gold apiece is what the house paid for the lot of us, which is the going rate for somebody who can't read what they're bound by."

"Ninety gold buys four of them out. Bring it here. Not for me — I've had mine. Then I'll come."

choices.label: I do not have ninety gold on me.
That is a great deal of money for four strangers.

kessa_return_paid.text:
She counts it, because she counts everything, and it takes a while, and she does not hurry it to be polite. Then it goes inside her shirt and she stands and gets the axe from behind the bar, where the innkeeper has been keeping it for her and asking no questions about that either.

"Right," Kessa says. "That's paper. Paper holds."

At the door she stops. "I'm not all right with you yet. I'd like that said out loud so neither of us has to guess at it. But I'll stand where you put me, same as before, and you can work the rest out on the road."

kessa_return_wait.text: "Then go and get it," Kessa says, with no edge on it at all. "I've been in this chair four days and I've nowhere I'm meant to be. It'll keep."

kessa_return_hard.text: "It isn't a grudge," Kessa says. "A grudge is free." She turns the cup. "Go on. The road's that way and it isn't getting shorter."

choices.label: All right. Say the number again.

kessa_close.text: "You keep your word," Kessa says, apropos of nothing, halfway through cleaning a gauntlet. "That's it. That's the whole of what I was going to say. I've been working out how to say it for about nine days."

Kessa has been about to say something for two days. You can watch her get to the front of it and then find a strap that needs doing. "Not yet," she says, when she catches you waiting. "I've nearly got it in an order."

"I've worked out what it is," Kessa says, apropos of nothing, over the top of the gauntlet. "It's that I've never had to think past the end of a contract before and I've started doing it, and it's making me clumsy, and I've decided to tell you that rather than be clumsy quietly."
Kessa looks at you a long moment over the gauntlet, and lets whatever it was go by. "Another night," she says, and means it kindly.

romance_after.text: Kessa has taken to doing the last of the whetstone work sitting against your side, which she has never once announced and would deny is an arrangement. The rhythm of it slows when she is about to say something and doesn't, and then picks back up, content.

"Middle bit's going better than advertised," Kessa says, to the fire, in the tone of a report. She checks you've heard it, once, sideways, and goes back to the gauntlet. The stone keeps its rhythm the whole time, which from her is a whole letter.

She has started leaving the axe on your side of the fire at night. Asked about it once, she said somebody careful should sleep near it, and got very interested in a strap. The axe has been eleven years in her keeping and has never once been out of her reach before.
Kessa moves the whetstone kit six inches along the log, which is her way of making room.
